introduction-magpies-vs-engineers.core: Curiosity draws engineers to shiny new tech, but every unfamiliar technology carries hidden operational cost. Choosing new tech should be a deliberate investment, not a reflex.

first_principles.problem: New projects adopt the trendiest framework, database and cloud service all at once, and the team spends its time fighting unknown failure modes instead of shipping.
truths: New tech has undiscovered bugs and sparse docs.
Teams have limited capacity to learn and operate.
derivation: Treat novelty as a **cost** to justify.
Spend novelty where it **differentiates** the product.

analogy.title: Magpies collecting shiny things
analogy.story: A magpie grabs anything that glitters, whether useful or not. An engineer should pick tools for the job.
analogy.breaks: Magpies pay nothing to keep shiny objects. Teams pay maintenance on every tool.

example.title: A new service with five new technologies
example.scenario: New language, DB, queue, framework and deploy tool.

check.q: Why is curiosity without discipline costly?
check.a: Each new technology brings unknown failure modes and learning costs the team must absorb.

the-theory-of-innovation-tokens.core: You get about three innovation tokens for your whole stack (Dan McKinley). Each represents your team's limited capacity to absorb unproven technology; spend them only where they buy real advantage.

first_principles.problem: Without a budget, teams adopt novelty everywhere, and capacity to operate the system runs out.
truths: Capacity to absorb new tech is finite.
derivation: Each new, poorly understood technology **costs one**.

analogy.title: A limited budget of risky bets
analogy.story: With three lottery tickets, you'd think hard about which draws to enter.
analogy.breaks: Tokens aren't literal; the point is scarcity, not the exact number.

example.title: A video startup's stack
example.outcome: the team innovates where it matters and stays operable elsewhere.

check.q: What does an innovation token represent?
check.a: A unit of the team's limited capacity to absorb the cost of unproven technology.

boring-technology-is-a-superpower.core: Boring means proven: its bugs are found, its edges documented and its tooling mature. Choosing it outsources your problem-solving to the whole industry.

first_principles.problem: Teams dismiss Postgres or cron as 'old', then spend months debugging a new tool whose failure modes nobody has seen.
truths: Mature tech has known failure modes.
Hiring for common tech is easier.
derivation: Value **known failure modes** over new features.
Count **community, hiring and tooling** as features.

analogy.title: A well-travelled road
analogy.story: A busy road has signs, petrol stations and mechanics. A brand-new shortcut might be faster, but if you break down, nobody is there.
analogy.breaks: Roads don't improve themselves. Boring tech keeps improving through its community.

example.title: Postgres vs a new distributed DB
example.scenario: A small team needs a primary store.
example.outcome: the team spends time on product, not obscure bugs.

check.q: What does 'boring' mean in this context?
check.a: Proven and well understood, with known failure modes and mature tooling.

the-hidden-costs-of-novelty.core: A technology's visible costs (licences, hosting) are the tip of the iceberg. Below lie learning, tooling gaps, monitoring, hiring, security patching, integration and the cost of being first to find bugs.

first_principles.problem: Teams compare benchmarks and features, then discover months of hidden costs operating the new tool.
derivation: List **hidden** costs: learning curve, monitoring, backups, upgrades, hiring, security, integration, debugging unknowns.

analogy.title: An iceberg
analogy.story: Only a small part shows above water; the bulk that sinks ships is below.
analogy.breaks: Icebergs are passive. Hidden costs keep growing as the tool is used more.

example.title: Adopting a new graph database

steps.label: Reality
steps.detail: The team built backup and monitoring tooling themselves.

example.outcome: you estimate the full iceberg before choosing.

check.q: Name three hidden costs of a new technology.
check.a: Learning curve, missing monitoring/backup tooling, and hiring difficulty.

when-to-spend-a-token-and-when-to-save-i.core: Spend a token only when the problem is core to your business, existing tools genuinely can't solve it, and the benefit is large enough to justify ongoing cost. Otherwise, save it.

first_principles.problem: Teams spend tokens on peripheral problems (a fancy logging system) and have none left for what actually differentiates them.
truths: Tokens spent can't easily be recovered.

analogy.title: Spending savings
analogy.story: You'd spend savings on something that changes your life, not on a fancier toaster.
analogy.breaks: Savings can be rebuilt. Tokens are freed only by making a tech boring (learning it) or removing it.

example.title: Two token requests
example.scenario: A real-time pricing engine vs a new logging pipeline.

steps.label: Decision
steps.detail: One token spent; logging uses the existing stack.

points: Tokens free up as tech matures.

check.q: What are the three conditions for spending a token?
check.a: The problem is core, boring tools can't solve it, and the benefit clearly exceeds the cost.

innovation-tokens-in-platform-engineerin.core: Platform teams are especially tempted by novel infrastructure, and their choices impose costs on every product team. Spend platform tokens on what improves developer experience, keep the substrate boring, and offer paved roads.

first_principles.problem: A platform team adopts a service mesh, a new GitOps tool and an exotic database. Product teams inherit the complexity and the platform team drowns in support.
truths: Engineers are vocal about exciting tech.
Developer experience is the platform's product.
derivation: Spend tokens on **developer-facing value** (self-service, fast feedback).
Offer **paved roads** and limit supported options.
Evaluate novelty by **impact on product teams**.

analogy.title: A city's utilities
analogy.story: Citizens want reliable water and power, not experimental pipes. Innovation goes into services people notice.
analogy.breaks: Utilities serve passive users. Developers actively push for new tools, so platform teams need firm criteria.

example.title: Service mesh proposal

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Token saved for a self-service environments feature.

example.outcome: the platform stays reliable and developers get features they notice.

check.q: Why are innovation tokens especially important for platform teams?
check.a: Their technology choices impose costs on every team that uses the platform.
